Good afternoon, and thank you for the opportunity. I am Jiaying Li, currently completing the MRes in Urban Spatial Science at UCL CASA. I will introduce myself through four connected parts: my education, selected research outputs, the research I propose for the PhD, and my future plans.

[Sources]

???
My education combines architecture and urban spatial science. Tsinghua and BUCEA trained me to work with spatial form, material systems, urban context and implementation. CASA made these questions measurable through geospatial data, remote sensing, spatial statistics and urban modelling. The personality map is retained from my portfolio because it describes how I work: curiosity defines the question, systematic thinking structures the evidence, and adaptability supports iteration under uncertainty.

[Sources]
Academic facts and research outputs: latest applicant CV, published at https://jiaying-ice.github.io/Jiaying-portfolio/CASA_WORK/CV_Jiaying_LI.pdf
Portrait and personal portfolio material: author-provided assets.
Dr Jinda Qi profile: https://cde.nus.edu.sg/arch/staffs/qi-jinda/

<div class="design-takeaway"><b>SPATIAL FORM</b><span>+</span><b>ENVIRONMENTAL PERFORMANCE</b><span>+</span><b>IMPLEMENTATION</b></div>

???
Design was my starting point. It trained me to move between the scale of a component, a building and an urban system while keeping implementation in view. During an internship, one project was constructed and exhibited at the ninth Bi-City Biennale of Urbanism and Architecture in Shenzhen. This experience still shapes how I approach research: evidence should eventually inform something that can be designed, operated or changed.

Portfolio images and linked portfolio PDF: author-provided portfolio repository, https://github.com/JIAYING-ICE/Jiaying-portfolio
Course and studio results: latest applicant CV.

???
CASA extended my design training into a research toolkit. I use geospatial data to observe conditions, spatial analysis to measure patterns and uncertainty, and simulation to test explanations or alternatives. Together, these capabilities support research on built-environment performance across sustainability, health, energy transition and climate resilience. The full thirty-six-node map and six inspected coursework outputs remain available through the interactive tabs.

[Sources]
CASA curriculum and coursework: author-provided course materials and portfolio repository.

Community-scale BIPV renovation presents a decision problem: energy, carbon and financial priorities can favour different designs. For a seventy-nine-unit community, we compared fifteen configurations using ray-traced solar analysis, EnergyPlus, lifecycle carbon and financial evaluation. The result was three policy-conditional optima—commercial, balanced and carbon-leading—rather than one imposed ranking. As equal first author, I led the integrated spatial, energy and multi-criteria analysis. The TAKE AWAY was that transparent criteria turn technical performance into a policy-relevant choice.

[Sources]

???
The cardiac-emergency study asked how visible infrastructure aligns with operational performance across cities. The evidence covered one point eight two one million STEMI records, four thousand two hundred and fifty-nine centres and three hundred and fifty cities. Pre-hospital and in-hospital performance diverged in one hundred and ninety cities, and operational variables accounted for sixty-nine percent of the fitted model's SHAP-based predictive contribution—a predictive rather than causal interpretation. As second author, I contributed data curation, spatial and statistical analysis, and interpretable modelling. The TAKE AWAY was that separating infrastructure from operations reveals distinct governance priorities.

<div class="status-line">MRes dissertation · Manuscript in preparation · First author</div>

???
My MRes addressed a measurement problem: deployment maps show where PV is visible, while planning requires comparison with building-level opportunity over time. I integrated repeated imagery, official footprints and LiDAR across one hundred and sixty thousand nine hundred and fifty-nine buildings. Among forty thousand two hundred and forty buildings in the upper opportunity quartile, seven thousand five hundred and ninety-eight had model-indicated PV. The controlled temporal subset retained three thousand five hundred and forty records, including eight hundred and seventy-four high-opportunity buildings with no PV observed by 2025. I independently owned the full workflow from question definition to sensitivity analysis. The TAKE AWAY was that denominator, scale and temporal evidence can shape the conclusion as strongly as the detection model.

[Sources]
Source dissertation: Measuring Rooftop Solar Deployment–Opportunity Alignment: A Building-Level Spatial Analysis with Temporal Identification in Washington, DC.
Figures: final dissertation figures 1.1, 3.2, 3.3, 4.1, 4.2 and 4.3 from the author-controlled final figure package.

## Research Motivation | Humid-heat recovery unfolds across connected scales

<div class="proposal-id"><b>Urban Humid-Heat Persistence and Recovery in Singapore</b> · Mechanisms, Model Sufficiency and Functional Significance</div>

<div class="motivation-layout">
  <div class="proposal-figure large"><img class="zoomable svg-source" src="images/research_outputs/proposal/proposal_event_time_framework.svg" alt="Event-time framework for regional, local and building recovery"></div>
  <div class="scale-stack"><div class="proposal-opening"><label>STARTING QUESTION</label><b>What happens after the regional weather appears to improve?</b></div><div class="scale-card regional"><b>Regional forcing</b><span>Defines the shared meteorological event and the onset of regional relaxation.</span></div><div class="scale-card local"><b>Local humid heat</b><span>Measures neighbourhood decay, sustained clearance, rebound and carry-over.</span></div><div class="scale-card building"><b>Building protection</b><span>Evaluates indoor thermal protection, lag and functional recovery.</span></div><div class="motivation-question prominent"><label>RESEARCH FOCUS</label>Which differences recur, which processes explain them, and what evidence is useful for building and operational decisions?</div></div>
</div>

<div class="concept-note">Conceptual event clock · timing relationships are categorical.</div>

???
The proposal begins with a simple question: What happens after the regional weather appears to improve? In Singapore, regional forcing may relax while some neighbourhoods remain warm and humid, and buildings may recover later. I place three transitions on one event clock: regional relaxation, local decline and sustained clearance, and building thermal-protection recovery. The figure defines comparable timings without pre-judging the result. Singapore is a strong test case because humidity, coastal circulation, dense morphology and managed cooling interact within one compact city.

[Sources]
Verified PhD proposal: Urban Humid-Heat Persistence and Recovery in Singapore: Mechanisms, Model Sufficiency and Functional Significance.
Figure: original SVG, Figure 2 event-time framework, author-provided final submission package.

## Research Questions

<div class="rq-progression">
  <div class="rq-card rq1"><div class="rq-label">RQ1 · MEASURE</div><b>Recurring spatial recovery</b><p>Which local recovery differences recur across events after accounting for event conditions?</p><span>Outcome: forcing-aware recovery measures and recurrent spatial patterns</span></div>
  <div class="rq-link">→</div>
  <div class="rq-card rq2"><div class="rq-label">RQ2 · EXPLAIN</div><b>Processes and model sufficiency</b><p>Which atmospheric and urban processes are consistent with recurrent differences, and when does WRF-Urban add evidence?</p><span>Outcome: targeted process tests and comparative model evidence</span></div>
  <div class="rq-link">→</div>
  <div class="rq-card rq3"><div class="rq-label">RQ3 · RELATE</div><b>Building thermal significance</b><p>When do outdoor recovery differences translate into lagged or decoupled building thermal protection, and what does this imply for building operation or heat-response timing?</p><span>Outcome: outdoor–building recovery relationships with operational meaning</span></div>
</div>

<div class="rq-foundation"><div><b>Common event clock</b><span>Comparable timing across regional, local and building scales</span></div><div><b>Independent observations</b><span>Outcome definition before targeted model experiments</span></div><div><b>Comparative evidence</b><span>Model complexity evaluated by the information it adds</span></div></div>

???
The research is organised through three questions. First, which local recovery differences recur across events after accounting for event conditions? Second, which atmospheric and urban processes are consistent with those recurring differences, and when does WRF-Urban add useful evidence? Third, when do outdoor recovery differences translate into lagged or decoupled building thermal protection? The sequence moves from measurement, to explanation, to functional significance, with independent observations defining the recovery outcomes.

[Sources]
Research questions and outcome definitions: author-provided verified PhD proposal.

???
The design begins with observations. Atmospheric data define events and recovery outcomes, urban surface and form data describe local context, and building records provide the functional interface where access and approvals permit. Targeted WRF and WRF-Urban experiments then test process explanations. Historical forecast records support a later replay analysis. The comparison evaluates weather skill, urban information skill, and functional or decision relevance. Each data source therefore has a specific analytical role, and partnership-dependent data are identified explicitly.

  <div class="year-card y2"><div class="year-top"><span>YEAR 2 · IDENTIFY</span><b>Identify recurring spatial differences</b></div><div class="year-row"><label>RESEARCH FOCUS</label><p>Use multiple events to distinguish recurring neighbourhood patterns from event-specific variation.</p></div><div class="year-row output"><label>OUTPUTS</label><p>Multi-event analysis · recovery maps · Papers 1–2 · frozen WRF configuration</p></div><div class="year-contribution"><label>CONTRIBUTION</label><p>Evidence on which recovery differences persist across events.</p></div></div>
  <div class="year-card y3"><div class="year-top"><span>YEAR 3 · EXPLAIN</span><b>Explain processes and compare models</b></div><div class="year-row"><label>RESEARCH FOCUS</label><p>Test atmospheric clearance, local heat–moisture memory and urban form using matched models.</p></div><div class="year-row output"><label>OUTPUTS</label><p>Process experiments · fair model comparison · building trajectories · Paper 3</p></div><div class="year-contribution"><label>CONTRIBUTION</label><p>Evidence on why recovery differs and when detailed modelling is useful.</p></div></div>
  <div class="year-card y4"><div class="year-top"><span>YEAR 4 · APPLY</span><b>Connect recovery to buildings and decisions</b></div><div class="year-row"><label>RESEARCH FOCUS</label><p>Relate outdoor recovery to thermal protection and test historical forecast information where archives permit.</p></div><div class="year-row output"><label>OUTPUTS</label><p>Outdoor–building study · retrospective forecast test · Paper 4 · thesis · archive · practitioner brief</p></div><div class="year-contribution"><label>CONTRIBUTION</label><p>Evidence for protection and operational timing in warm-humid cities.</p></div></div>

    <tr><td><b>2</b></td><td>Cross-event inference · conditional spatial account · hindcast</td><td>Extend multi-event environmental and building observations; estimate recurrent spatial differences and weather-regime interactions; continue monitoring; evaluate and freeze the principal WRF configuration.</td><td>Event imbalance; spatial-support sensitivity; incomplete process observations; structural model uncertainty.</td><td>Paper 1 submission · Paper 2 on recurring spatial recovery and weather-regime dependence · frozen WRF configuration.</td></tr>

???
Over four years, the project moves from defining recovery to explaining it and testing why it matters. Year One establishes a clear event protocol and pilot trajectories. Year Two uses multiple events to identify which neighbourhood differences recur after weather conditions are considered. Year Three tests the atmospheric and urban processes behind those patterns and compares WRF-Urban with simpler methods. Year Four examines how outdoor recovery relates to building thermal protection and, where suitable archives exist, whether earlier information could improve protection timing. Together, these stages produce four linked studies, a reproducible dataset and method, documented code, a thesis and a practitioner brief. The broader aim is to move urban heat assessment beyond peak maps towards evidence of when neighbourhoods and buildings have actually recovered.

I want to pursue a PhD for both personal and public reasons. I enjoy turning important urban questions into defensible evidence. Cities and buildings now face connected climate, energy and health pressures, and sustainable futures require a stronger evidence base linking spatial data, computation and environmental processes. NUS is an especially strong fit: Singapore combines humid tropical weather, coastal processes, dense urban form and managed cooling; NUS and CDE offer an interdisciplinary research environment and doctoral support; and Dr Jinda Qi's work connects urban heat, computational design and AI-driven built-environment design. Singapore's safety, stability and international connectivity also support sustained research. Post-PhD, I hope to build an academic career at the intersection of the built environment, urban climate and human well-being, translating research findings into practical decisions and real-world applications. Thank you for your time and consideration. I look forward to our discussion.
